newsitem.title: USA: N.J. $3.4 bln bond deal faces several obstacles.
newsitem.headline: N.J. $3.4 bln bond deal faces several obstacles.

text.p: New Jersey's proposal to borrow $3.4 billion to invest in the pension funds it operates for public employees still has significant hurdles to surmount.

It must pass muster with bond counsel, Wall Street and the Internal Revenue Service, Treasury spokesman Matt McDermott said. Then it must get majority votes in both chambers of the Legislature, where key Democratic leaders have blasted the idea since word of it leaked out over the weekend.

The taxable bond issue officially announced Monday would save the state about $623 million over two years. Gov. Whitman, who is seeking re-election this year, is scheduled to introduce her Fiscal Year 1998 budget Jan. 29.
Treasurer Brian Clymer said the 35-year bonds would not be tax free but would be backed by the state's full faith and credit. Pension assets would not be entailed, he said.

The idea is to raise enough capital to close the gap between the nearly $48 billion in assets in the four funds and their current obligations, McDermott said. That would free up $2.3 billion in current surplus.

The state operates pension funds for 433,300 active workers and 154,500 retirees. These include employees of state, county and local governments and the public schools. They contribute between five and seven percent of salary to retirement benefits, varying with seniority.
The plan is to use the surplus to pay $354 million of the $623 million in state contributions in Fiscal Year 1998 and to reduce the contribution in the current budget by $269 million.
"Our goal is to have this in place by May, so it can be kept separate from the budget," McDermott said.

The financial maneuver is an attempt to capitalize on the strong performance of the pension fund's investment portfolio. Its return has averaged 12.4 percent since recovering from the 1981-82 recession, while the borrowing would cost no more than 8.75 percent, state officials said.

Former Gov. Jim Florio had converted the pension funds' portfolios from book to market value in 1991, and the Whitman administration had restated their actuarial bases in 1994. That enabled it to reduce the annual contribution by nearly $700 million a year in its FY 1995 budget, and actuaries agreed that this would have to be made up starting early in the next century.
Consultants for the public employee unions, which opposed the maneuver, said the estimates relied upon by Clymer were too optimistic about continued performance in the investment portfolio.
